etymology: Hebrew Ya’zer, “he helps” or “helpful,” a city of Gilead east of the Jordan.
biblical_def: Jazer was a city of Gilead, east of the Jordan, taken from the Amorites in the days of Moses. When Israel turned to possess the land of Sihon, Moses sent to spy out Jazer, and they took its villages and drove out the Amorites that were there (Num 21:32). The land of Jazer and Gilead was a place of rich pasture, and when the children of Reuben and Gad saw that it was good for cattle, they asked Moses to give them their inheritance on that side of Jordan (Num 32:1–5). The town was rebuilt by Gad and at length given with its suburbs to the Levites of the family of Merari (Josh 21:39). In the latter days the prophets named the “sea of Jazer” and the vine of Sibmah in their lament over fallen Moab (Jer 48:32). Among David’s officers were mighty men of Hebron found at Jazer of Gilead (1Ch 26:31). The name means “he helps,” a fitting confession for a people whose help was in the name of the LORD. Jazer stands among the eastern cities that Reuben and Gad asked for their flocks, a place that tested whether the two tribes would still cross over to fight for their brethren’s inheritance — which, to their honour, they did.
webster_summary: A city of Gilead east of Jordan, taken from the Amorites; a place of rich pasture sought by Reuben and Gad.

corruption_summary: A place-name, not a doctrine in dispute; its lesson tests whether God’s people will still labour for their brethren’s good.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the duty of the two and a half tribes who settled at Jazer and the eastern pastures: though they had their inheritance, they were bound to cross over armed and fight until their brethren also possessed the land (Num 32:20–22). The believer at ease must not forget the warfare of the whole people of God; rest for oneself is no release from labour for others.

Jazer, “he helps,” also confesses where Israel’s true help lay. The rich pastures might feed their flocks, but their help was in the name of the LORD who made heaven and earth. The eastern tribes were later the first to be carried away captive, a warning that the choicest pasture is no security when a people drift from the God who is their help.

etymology: Hebrew Yahats, perhaps “a place trodden down” or “a battlefield,” a town in the plain east of Jordan.
biblical_def: Jahaz was a town on the tableland east of the Jordan, remembered chiefly as the place where Sihon king of the Amorites met Israel in battle and was overthrown. When Israel asked leave to pass peaceably through his land, Sihon would not suffer them, but gathered all his people and came out against them into the wilderness; he came to Jahaz and fought against Israel, and Israel smote him with the edge of the sword and possessed his land from Arnon unto Jabbok (Num 21:23–24). The victory at Jahaz opened the whole country of Sihon to the tribes of Reuben and Gad, and the town itself fell within the inheritance of Reuben (Josh 13:18). It was afterward given with its suburbs to the Levites of the family of Merari (Josh 21:36). In later ages, when Moab held the land, the prophets named Jahaz in their burdens against Moab, for its cry was heard in the day of that nation’s calamity (Isa 15:4; Jer 48:34). Jahaz thus marks the first great conquest east of Jordan, the opening blow by which the LORD began to give His people the land of the Amorite. It witnesses that when the enemies of God’s people refuse them peace and come out to battle, the LORD delivers the proud into the hands of His own.
webster_summary: A town on the eastern tableland where Sihon the Amorite fought Israel and was overthrown.

corruption_summary: A place-name, not a doctrine in dispute; its lesson is that the LORD delivers the proud who refuse His people peace.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the overthrow of Sihon at Jahaz. Israel sought to pass in peace, but Sihon hardened his heart and came out to war; and the LORD delivered him into Israel’s hand. The proud who set themselves against the people of God, refusing every offer of peace, are broken; the battle they choose becomes their ruin.

Jahaz, the first great victory east of Jordan, also displays the faithfulness of God in beginning to give His people the land of promise. What He had sworn to Abraham He performed, town by town and battle by battle. The conquest was no accident of war but the unfolding of an ancient covenant, and Jahaz was its opening blow on the eastern side.

etymology: Hebrew Qedemoth, “eastern parts” or “beginnings,” a town and wilderness east of the Jordan in Reuben.
biblical_def: Kedemoth was a town on the eastern tableland that fell to the tribe of Reuben (Josh 13:18), and it gave its name to the wilderness from which Moses sent messengers of peace to Sihon king of Heshbon. “I sent messengers out of the wilderness of Kedemoth unto Sihon king of Heshbon with words of peace,” Moses recounted, asking only to pass along the highway and to buy meat and water for silver (Deut 2:26–28). Sihon refused, for the LORD his God had hardened his spirit and made his heart obstinate, that He might deliver him into Israel’s hand (Deut 2:30); and so the battle of Jahaz followed. The town of Kedemoth was afterward given with its suburbs to the Levites of the family of Merari (Josh 21:37). Its name, “eastern parts,” suits a place on the sunrise edge of the land. Kedemoth is remembered as the place from which Israel sought peace before war, offering Sihon a way of life that he despised. It witnesses that the people of God are to seek peace where they may, but that the obstinate refusal of the wicked, hardened by the just judgment of God, brings them to the destruction they have chosen.
webster_summary: A Reubenite town and wilderness east of Jordan, from which Moses sent words of peace to Sihon.

corruption_summary: A place-name, not a doctrine in dispute; its lesson is that God’s people seek peace, yet the obstinate are hardened to their ruin.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is twofold. First, Israel sent words of peace from Kedemoth before drawing the sword; the people of God are to seek peace where it may be had. Second, Sihon’s refusal was no mere stubbornness of man, for the LORD hardened his heart in righteous judgment, that He might deliver him up. The hardening of the wicked is itself within the just and sovereign rule of God.

Kedemoth thus touches the deep truth that the LORD reigns even over the rebellions of His enemies. Sihon despised the offered peace and was hardened to his destruction; yet his obstinacy did not thwart God’s purpose but fulfilled it. The Scripture teaches that the LORD hath made all things for Himself, yea, even the wicked for the day of evil (Prov 16:4), without Himself being the author of their sin.

etymology: Hebrew Betser, “a fortress” or “stronghold,” the city of refuge in the wilderness of Reuben.
biblical_def: Bezer was a city in the wilderness, in the plain country of the tribe of Reuben, east of the Jordan, appointed by Moses as one of the three cities of refuge on that side of the river (Deut 4:43). When Joshua confirmed the cities of refuge, he assigned Bezer in the wilderness upon the plain out of the tribe of Reuben, that the manslayer who killed unawares might flee thither and be safe from the avenger of blood until he stood before the congregation (Josh 20:8). Like the other refuge-cities, it was also a Levitical town, given to the family of Merari (Josh 21:36). The name Bezer means “a fortress” or “stronghold,” and the city was indeed a stronghold of mercy: a fenced refuge where the guilty-yet-innocent might find shelter from vengeance. The three eastern cities — Bezer in Reuben, Ramoth in Gilead, Golan in Bashan — matched the three western, so that no Israelite, on whichever side of Jordan, was far from a place of refuge. Bezer pictures the gospel: a stronghold appointed by God, set within reach of every sinner, whither the soul pursued by the law’s avenger may flee and find safety in the appointed shelter, which is Christ the rock of our refuge.
webster_summary: A city of refuge in the wilderness plain of Reuben; a stronghold of mercy for the manslayer.

corruption_summary: A place-name, not a doctrine in dispute; its lesson is the gospel pictured in the stronghold of refuge.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the mercy of the appointed refuge. Bezer, “the stronghold,” was set in the wilderness within reach of the manslayer, that he might flee from the avenger of blood and live. So Christ is the stronghold of the soul; the sinner, pursued by the just sentence of the law, flees to Him and is safe. The cities of refuge were no human invention but God’s own provision of mercy bounded by justice.

Bezer also teaches that the refuge availed only to the one who fled to it and abode within its walls; the manslayer who left the city before the death of the high priest was again exposed to the avenger. So there is no safety for the soul outside of Christ, nor for the one who, having fled to Him, turns back to the world. The refuge must be entered and kept; he that endureth to the end shall be saved.

etymology: Hebrew Beth-Nimrah, “house of sweet water” or “house of the leopard,” a fenced city built by Gad in the valley.
biblical_def: Beth-nimrah was a city in the valley east of the Jordan, in the well-watered land that the children of Gad asked for their inheritance and built up for themselves. When Reuben and Gad received their portion in the country of Sihon, the children of Gad built Beth-nimrah and Beth-haran as fenced cities, with folds for their sheep (Num 32:36). The town lay in the rich valley near the Jordan, named among the cities of the rest of the kingdom of Sihon that fell to Gad, from the valley up to the edge of the sea of Chinnereth (Josh 13:27). Its name is read as “house of sweet water,” fitting a place of springs and good pasture, or “house of the leopard,” perhaps for the wild beasts of the thickets along the river. Beth-nimrah is little mentioned, yet it stands among the fenced cities and sheepfolds that the eastern tribes built for their families and flocks before they crossed over armed to fight for their brethren’s inheritance. It witnesses the settled provision the LORD made for His people in the good land east of Jordan, and the order by which they housed their little ones and their cattle in safety before going to war — care for the household joined to readiness for the battle.
webster_summary: A fenced city built by Gad in the valley east of Jordan, in a land of springs and good pasture.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the order of the eastern tribes who built Beth-nimrah and its sister-cities. They housed their little ones and their flocks in fenced safety, and then crossed over armed to fight for their brethren. Provision for the family and readiness for the warfare of God’s people are not at odds; the godly man cares for his own household and yet does not excuse himself from the common battle.

Beth-nimrah, “house of sweet water,” also stands as a token of the LORD’s good provision. He gave His people a land of springs and pasture, fenced cities and folds, that they might dwell in safety. Every settled blessing of the believer’s life is from the same gracious hand; the sweet waters are His gift, and the house is built by His favour.

etymology: Hebrew Aro’er, perhaps “ruins” or “bare height,” a town on the brink of the river Arnon.
biblical_def: Aroer was a town on the bank of the river Arnon, on the very edge of the deep gorge that formed the southern border of the land Israel took from Sihon. It was the southernmost landmark of the Transjordan conquest: “From Aroer, which is by the brink of the river of Arnon, and from the city that is by the river, even unto Gilead, there was not one city too strong for us: the LORD our God delivered all unto us” (Deut 2:36). The town and its region fell to the tribe of Reuben, whose coast began from Aroer on the bank of the Arnon (Josh 13:16), and it was built up by the children of Gad as well (Num 32:34). When Jephthah disputed with the king of Ammon, he pleaded Israel’s three hundred years’ dwelling in Heshbon and Aroer and their towns as proof of rightful possession (Judg 11:26). The name Aroer, “ruins” or “bare height,” suits a stark town on the rim of a great ravine. Aroer is remembered as the boundary-stone of the eastern inheritance, the place from which the LORD’s gift of the land was measured, and a standing witness that not one city was too strong for the God who delivered all into His people’s hand.
webster_summary: A town on the brink of the river Arnon, the southern boundary of Israel’s land east of Jordan.

corruption_summary: A place-name, not a doctrine in dispute; its lesson is that no stronghold is too strong for the God who gives His people the land.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the testimony of Deuteronomy: from Aroer onward, “there was not one city too strong for us: the LORD our God delivered all unto us.” The strength of the enemy’s walls is nothing against the arm of the LORD. The believer facing strongholds of sin or opposition may take heart that no fortress stands when God has decreed its fall.

Aroer as a boundary-stone also bears witness to the rightful gift of God. Jephthah appealed to the long centuries of Israel’s dwelling from Aroer and Heshbon as proof that the land was theirs by the LORD’s grant, not by mere conquest. What God gives, He gives in truth; the inheritance of His people rests on His promise and His deed, and not on the shifting claims of the nations.

etymology: Hebrew Beth-ha-yeshimoth, “house of the wastes” or “place of deserts,” a town on the edge of the plains of Moab.
biblical_def: Beth-jeshimoth, “the house of the wastes,” lay at the lower end of the plains of Moab, near the northeastern shore of the salt sea, where Israel encamped in the last stage of the wilderness journey. There the people pitched by Jordan, “from Bethjesimoth even unto Abelshittim in the plains of Moab” (Num 33:49), in the broad camp from which they would cross over into the land. It was a solemn place, for it was in these plains of Moab, near Shittim, that Israel joined himself to Baal-peor and committed whoredom with the daughters of Moab, and the LORD sent a plague among them (Num 25). The town afterward fell within the inheritance of Reuben (Josh 13:20), and in the day of Moab’s judgment the prophet Ezekiel named Beth-jeshimoth among the frontier cities, “the glory of the country,” that should be opened to the spoiler (Ezek 25:9). The name, “house of the wastes,” fits a town on the rim of the desert by the dead waters of the salt sea. Beth-jeshimoth stands at the threshold of the promised land, a place of both expectation and warning: the last camp before the Jordan, and the scene of Israel’s grievous sin at Baal-peor.

corruption_summary: A place-name, not a doctrine in dispute; its lesson joins the threshold of promise to the warning of Baal-peor.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the double character of the plains of Moab where Beth-jeshimoth lay. It was the last camp before the inheritance, a place of expectation; yet there Israel fell into the idolatry and whoredom of Baal-peor and was struck by a plague. The nearness of the promise did not exempt the people from temptation; the very threshold of blessing was the scene of grievous sin. The believer near to his hope must watch and pray, lest he fall.

Beth-jeshimoth, “house of the wastes,” also reminds the reader that judgment came at last upon Moab, whose daughters had ensnared Israel. Ezekiel named the town among the cities to be opened to the spoiler. The nations that tempt the people of God to sin do not escape; the LORD remembers Baal-peor, and the house of the wastes was laid waste indeed.

etymology: Hebrew Sukkoth, “booths” or “shelters,” from sukkah, a booth; a town in the Jordan valley east of the river.
biblical_def: Succoth was a town in the valley of the Jordan, east of the river, in the portion of Gad (Josh 13:27). It took its name from the booths that Jacob made there: returning from Padan-aram after his wrestling at Peniel, Jacob journeyed to Succoth, and built him a house, and made booths for his cattle, “therefore the name of the place is called Succoth” (Gen 33:17). In the days of the judges, when Gideon pursued the kings of Midian with his three hundred faint yet pursuing, the men of Succoth refused to give bread to his weary band, mocking his unfinished victory; and when Gideon returned in triumph he chastised them, teaching the elders of the city with thorns of the wilderness and with briers (Judg 8:5–16). In Solomon’s reign the vessels of brass for the temple were cast in the clay ground of the Jordan plain between Succoth and Zarthan (1Ki 7:46). The name “booths” recalls the feast of tabernacles, when Israel dwelt in booths to remember the wilderness pilgrimage. Succoth witnesses both to the pilgrim life of God’s people, who have here no continuing city, and to the danger of withholding kindness from the LORD’s servants in the day of their labour.
webster_summary: A town in the Jordan valley named for Jacob’s booths; where the men refused bread to Gideon’s weary band.

And he took the elders of the city, and thorns of the wilderness and briers, and with them he taught the men of Succoth.

corruption_summary: A place-name, not a doctrine in dispute; its lesson joins the pilgrim life to the duty of kindness to God’s servants.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the warning of the men of Succoth, who withheld bread from Gideon’s faint band because they doubted his victory and feared the Midianites more than they honoured the LORD’s deliverer. To refuse kindness to the servants of God in the day of their labour, out of unbelief or self-interest, is no light thing; Gideon returned and taught them with briers. He that giveth a cup of cold water to a disciple shall not lose his reward, and he that refuses it answers for the slight.

Succoth, “booths,” also recalls the pilgrim character of God’s people. Jacob made booths there, temporary shelters for a journeying man; and Israel kept the feast of booths to remember that they were strangers and sojourners. The believer too dwells in booths, having here no continuing city, but seeking one to come. The name itself preaches that this world is a place of pilgrimage, not of permanent rest.
roots_summary: The name means “booths” or “shelters,” from sukkah, the booth of the feast of tabernacles.
roots_lines: Succoth — Hebrew Sukkoth, “booths” or “shelters.”
The singular sukkah is the booth of the feast of tabernacles.
Jacob named the place for the booths he made for his cattle.
It lay in the Jordan valley in the portion of Gad.
The town of booths preaches the pilgrim life of God’s people.
usage: Like the men of Succoth, those who withhold kindness from God’s servants answer for the slight.
Succoth, the town of booths, teaches that the believer dwells as a pilgrim with no continuing city.
Gideon’s briers at Succoth warn against doubting the LORD’s deliverer in the day of his labour.

etymology: Hebrew Ar, “a city,” the chief city of Moab, given by God to the children of Lot.
biblical_def: Ar, called Ar of Moab, was the chief city of the Moabites, on the river Arnon, and it stood as a marker of the land the LORD reserved to the descendants of Lot. When Israel came near the borders of Moab, the LORD commanded Moses, “Distress not the Moabites, neither contend with them in battle: for I will not give thee of their land for a possession; because I have given Ar unto the children of Lot for a possession” (Deut 2:9). Israel was to pass through Ar, the coast of Moab, buying meat and water, and not to provoke the people whose land was not theirs to take (Deut 2:18–29). The ancient song preserved in Numbers tells how a fire had gone out from Heshbon and consumed Ar of Moab when Sihon the Amorite had earlier wasted it (Num 21:28). In the prophets’ burden against Moab, Ar is named among the cities laid waste in the night of that nation’s calamity (Isa 15:1). Ar of Moab is remarkable as a city that Israel was forbidden to take, a witness that the LORD apportions to the nations their bounds, and that even the children of Lot held their land by the gift and decree of the God of Abraham.
webster_summary: The chief city of Moab on the Arnon; a land God forbade Israel to take, given to the children of Lot.
webster_full: AR OF MOAB, the chief city of the Moabites, upon the river Arnon.
The LORD gave Ar to the children of Lot and forbade Israel to take it (Deut 2:9).
Israel was to pass through Ar buying meat and water (Deut 2:18–29).
An ancient song told how fire from Heshbon had consumed Ar (Num 21:28).
The prophets named Ar among the cities laid waste in Moab’s judgment (Isa 15:1).
scriptures: Deut 2:9

And the LORD said unto me, Distress not the Moabites, neither contend with them in battle: for I will not give thee of their land for a possession; because I have given Ar unto the children of Lot for a possession.
Deut 2:18
Thou art to pass over through Ar, the coast of Moab, this day:
For there is a fire gone out of Heshbon, a flame from the city of Sihon: it hath consumed Ar of Moab, and the lords of the high places of Arnon.
Isa 15:1
The burden of Moab. Because in the night Ar of Moab is laid waste, and brought to silence; because in the night Kir of Moab is laid waste, and brought to silence;
corruption_summary: A place-name, not a doctrine in dispute; its lesson is that the LORD apportions to the nations their bounds.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sovereignty of God over the lands of the nations. Israel was forbidden to take Ar, for the LORD had given it to the children of Lot; the God who granted Canaan to Abraham’s seed also fixed the bounds of Moab and Edom and Ammon. He hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of the habitation of every people (Acts 17:26); the map of the nations is no accident but His decree.

Ar of Moab also teaches restraint under the command of God. Israel might have coveted the land of Moab, but the LORD said, “Distress not the Moabites,” and Israel obeyed. The people of God are to take only what God gives, and to leave untouched what He has reserved. Covetousness that reaches beyond the LORD’s grant, even toward a heathen people, is rebellion against His ordering hand.
roots_summary: The name Ar simply means “a city,” the chief city standing for the land of Moab.
roots_lines: Ar — Hebrew Ar, “a city.”
It was the chief city of Moab, called Ar of Moab.
It stood upon the river Arnon, the border of the land.
The LORD gave it to the children of Lot for a possession.
The chief city stood for the whole land Israel was forbidden to take.
usage: Like Israel forbidden to take Ar, the people of God take only what He gives and leave what He reserves.
Ar of Moab teaches that the LORD fixes the bounds of the habitation of every nation.
The forbidden city witnesses that covetousness beyond God’s grant is rebellion against His decree.

etymology: Hebrew Sela, “a rock” or “cliff,” the rock-fortress of Edom.
biblical_def: Sela, which means “a rock,” was the great rock-fortress of Edom, a stronghold set among the cliffs of the mountainous land of Esau, all but impregnable to its enemies. When Amaziah king of Judah warred against Edom, he slew ten thousand in the valley of salt and took Sela by war, and called the name of it Joktheel (2Ki 14:7). The prophet Isaiah, in his burden of Moab, bade the fugitives send the lamb of tribute to the ruler of the land “from Sela to the wilderness, unto the mount of the daughter of Zion” (Isa 16:1). The rock-city stood for the proud security of Edom, whose dwelling was in the clefts of the rock, who said in his heart, “Who shall bring me down to the ground?” (Obad 3). Yet the LORD declared that though Edom exalt himself as the eagle and set his nest among the stars, from thence He would bring him down (Obad 4). Sela thus became a parable of false security: a fortress that men thought no power could reach, yet which fell under the judgment of God. It witnesses that no rock, however high, can shelter the proud from the hand of the LORD, and that the only sure refuge is the Rock of Ages, the LORD Himself.
webster_summary: The rock-fortress of Edom among the cliffs; a parable of the proud security the LORD brings down.
webster_full: SELA, the rock-fortress of Edom among the mountain cliffs.
Its name signifies “a rock” or “cliff.”
Amaziah of Judah took it and called it Joktheel (2Ki 14:7).
Isaiah named it in his burden, sending tribute from Sela to Zion (Isa 16:1).
It stood for the proud security of Edom in the clefts of the rock (Obad 3).
scriptures: He slew of Edom in the valley of salt ten thousand, and took Selah by war, and called the name of it Joktheel unto this day.
Isa 16:1
Send ye the lamb to the ruler of the land from Sela to the wilderness, unto the mount of the daughter of Zion.
Obad 1:3
The pride of thine heart hath deceived thee, thou that dwellest in the clefts of the rock, whose habitation is high; that saith in his heart, Who shall bring me down to the ground?
Obad 1:4
Though thou exalt thyself as the eagle, and though thou set thy nest among the stars, thence will I bring thee down, saith the LORD.
corruption_summary: A place-name, not a doctrine in dispute; its lesson is that no rock can shelter the proud from the hand of God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the deceit of pride that dwells in the clefts of the rock and says, “Who shall bring me down?” Edom trusted in the height and strength of Sela, yet the LORD declared He would bring him down though he set his nest among the stars. No fortress of stone or of self-confidence can shelter the proud from the judgment of God; the higher the nest, the greater the fall.

Sela, “the rock,” also turns the heart to the true Rock. Edom’s rock failed him, but there is a Rock that does not fail: “the LORD is my rock, and my fortress” (Ps 18:2). The believer’s safety is not in any stronghold of his own making but in the Rock of Ages, cleft for him. The false security of Sela points by contrast to the only sure refuge of the soul.
roots_summary: The name means “a rock” or “cliff,” fitting a fortress hewn among the mountain crags of Edom.
roots_lines: Sela — Hebrew Sela, “a rock” or “cliff.”
It was the rock-fortress of Edom in the mountains of Esau.
Amaziah renamed it Joktheel after taking it by war.
Edom dwelt in the clefts of the rock in proud security.
The false rock of Edom points by contrast to the true Rock, the LORD.
usage: Like Edom in Sela, the proud who trust their stronghold are brought down by the hand of God.
Sela teaches that no fortress of stone or self-confidence shelters the soul from judgment.
The failing rock of Edom turns the heart to the Rock of Ages, the only sure refuge.
